title: Where Do Ideas Come From? And How Do Entrepreneurs Keep Them Flowing?
author: Idea Incubator, MGIT
excerpt: Most businesses don't begin with a million-dollar idea. They begin with something much smaller — a problem someone notices, a question that keeps coming back, or an everyday situation that could work better.
content:
Most businesses don't begin with a million-dollar idea. They often begin with something much smaller: a problem someone notices, a question that keeps coming back, or an everyday situation that could work better.

A student struggling to find affordable food near campus, a shop owner spending hours managing orders manually, or a customer frustrated by a complicated booking process may all be experiencing the beginning of an entrepreneurial idea. The difference is that an entrepreneur doesn't stop at noticing the problem. They start asking, "Could this be done differently?"

## Ideas Rarely Come Out of Nowhere

We often think of ideas as sudden flashes of inspiration, but they rarely appear from nowhere.

Our brains constantly collect information from our experiences, conversations, observations, and the things we learn. When these pieces of information connect in new ways, they can become ideas.

In entrepreneurship, this ability to connect seemingly unrelated things can turn an ordinary observation into a potential opportunity.

This is why entrepreneurs can find inspiration in places that don't seem directly related to business. A conversation with a customer might reveal a problem they had never considered. A book about another industry might introduce a completely different business model. A personal inconvenience might reveal a problem shared by thousands of other people.

Reading widely, listening to different perspectives, and learning from different fields gives our minds more building blocks to work with.

## Start With a Problem, Not a Business Idea

Noticing a problem is only the beginning. The next challenge is generating possible solutions.

Instead of immediately trying to find one perfect business idea, entrepreneurs can give themselves a fixed amount of time to generate as many possibilities as possible.

The important part is to avoid judging the ideas while generating them. At this stage, even an unrealistic idea can be useful because it may lead to a more practical one.

For example, imagine a student notices that many college students struggle to find people who can help them learn skills outside their academic courses. Brainstorming could take that thought further: a skill-sharing platform, peer tutoring, short weekend courses, student mentorship, or a marketplace where students exchange skills instead of money.

The first idea doesn't have to be the final business. The goal is to create enough possibilities to discover where the real opportunity might be.

## Use Structured Creativity to Generate Better Ideas

Sometimes, entrepreneurs don't need to invent something completely new. They can create value by improving something that already exists.

This is where SCAMPER can be particularly useful. SCAMPER provides seven ways to rethink an existing product, service, or business idea:

S — Substitute · C — Combine · A — Adapt · M — Modify · P — Put to another use · E — Eliminate · R — Reverse or Rearrange

Instead of waiting for inspiration, SCAMPER gives entrepreneurs a structured way to challenge what already exists.

![SCAMPER in action — structured creativity](/images/ideas-blog-2.png)

## SCAMPER in Action

Consider a simple example: an entrepreneur wants to improve the experience of attending college events.

What could they Substitute? Physical registration could be replaced with QR-based registration. What could they Combine? Registration, event schedules, networking, and feedback could be brought together on one platform. What could they Adapt? A live-tracking feature similar to food-delivery apps could show students where an event is happening or whether it has started. What could they Eliminate? Unnecessary forms and repetitive registration steps could be removed. What could they Reverse or Rearrange? Instead of making students search for events themselves, the platform could provide personalised event recommendations.

One ordinary problem has now produced several possible business directions. That is the value of structured creativity: it gives entrepreneurs better questions to ask instead of waiting for inspiration to arrive on its own.

## Why One Good Idea Isn't Enough

Generating one good idea isn't enough to become entrepreneurial.

Ideas need to keep flowing because the first idea may not be the right one, and the first version of a solution may not work. This is why developing consistent habits matters.

One simple habit is maintaining an idea bank. Whenever an interesting problem, observation, customer complaint, or possible solution comes to mind, write it down. It doesn't need to be a complete business plan. A single sentence can be enough. Over time, these small observations can become a collection of opportunities worth exploring.

## Stay Curious and Keep Questioning

Another important habit is staying curious. Entrepreneurs constantly question the way things work: Why does this process take so long? Why is this product expensive? Why do customers have to take so many steps to complete a simple task? What happens if one step is removed? Could a solution from another industry work here?

Asking these questions trains us to look beyond what already exists. Curiosity turns everyday experiences into potential sources of innovation.

## Look Beyond Your Own Industry

Curiosity becomes even more powerful when it is combined with different experiences. If we only consume information from our own field, we may keep approaching problems in familiar ways.

Exploring other industries, talking to people with different experiences, reading widely, and collaborating with others can introduce completely new perspectives. A solution that works in one industry might inspire an entirely different solution in another.

## Give Your Brain Room to Think

There is also an entrepreneurial lesson in something that doesn't look productive at all: downtime.

When our minds are constantly occupied, there is little space for unexpected connections. Walking, journaling, resting, or simply allowing yourself to think without a specific task can create room for ideas to develop.

Building an environment that supports curiosity and reflection can help keep the creative process active. Not every productive moment has to look like work.

## Don't Reject an Idea Too Early

Most importantly, entrepreneurs need to become comfortable with imperfect ideas. If every thought is immediately rejected because it sounds unrealistic, expensive, or strange, many potentially useful ideas will never develop.

An idea doesn't have to be perfect when it first appears. It can be questioned, tested, modified, combined with another idea, improved, or completely changed. The goal isn't to protect the first idea. The goal is to discover whether there is something valuable hidden inside it.

## Where Creativity Meets Entrepreneurship

This is where creativity and entrepreneurship meet. Creativity helps us imagine possibilities, while entrepreneurship pushes us to ask whether those possibilities can solve a real problem and create value.

Having ideas is only one part of entrepreneurial thinking. Learning how to recognise opportunities, develop possibilities, and eventually test them is what turns creativity into action.

## The Question That Starts It All

The next time you find yourself searching for a great business idea, don't begin by asking "What startup should I build?" Instead, start by paying attention to the world around you. Notice what frustrates people, what takes too long, what feels unnecessarily complicated, what people repeatedly complain about, and what could be made easier, faster, cheaper, or more accessible.

Once you notice a problem, give yourself permission to explore it from different angles. Brainstorm possible solutions without immediately judging them, use SCAMPER to challenge existing approaches, write down interesting observations, and talk to people who experience the problem themselves.

This is what makes entrepreneurial thinking different from simply having random ideas. An entrepreneur learns to look at ordinary situations with curiosity and ask whether there is an opportunity hidden inside the problem.

The idea doesn't have to be perfect at the beginning. It can start as a question, develop into a possibility, and eventually become a solution that creates real value.

After all, entrepreneurial ideas don't always come from extraordinary moments. Sometimes, they begin with something completely ordinary — a problem that everyone has noticed but nobody has tried to solve differently.

And sometimes, the first step towards building something meaningful is simply asking: "What if there's a better way?"

title: Validation: Testing Ideas in the Real World
author: Idea Incubator, MGIT
excerpt: Just because an idea sounds promising doesn't mean people will actually use it. Before investing significant time, money, and effort into building a business, entrepreneurs need to find out whether their ideas solve real problems for real people.
content:
## What If Your Brilliant Startup Idea Isn't What People Need?

Every startup begins with an idea. Sometimes, it comes from noticing a problem people face every day. Other times, it comes from a personal experience, a conversation, or simply asking, "What if there were a better way to do this?"

But here's the important question: Just because an idea sounds promising doesn't mean people will actually use it.

Imagine spending months developing an app, designing its features, and preparing to launch it, only to discover that your target audience doesn't need it as much as you expected. You might have a great concept, but without understanding your customers, even the most exciting idea can struggle to succeed.

This is where validation comes in.

In our previous blog, we explored ideation — the process of discovering problems, brainstorming possibilities, and generating startup ideas. But having an idea is only the beginning. Before investing significant time, money, and effort into building a business, entrepreneurs need to find out whether their ideas solve real problems for real people.

Validation helps them do exactly that.

![The validation journey: six steps from understanding the problem to creating real value](/images/validation-blog-2.jpg)

## 1. Start With the Problem, Not Your Assumptions

One of the biggest mistakes aspiring entrepreneurs make is falling in love with their ideas before understanding the problems they are trying to solve.

When an idea feels exciting, it is easy to assume that everyone else will find it equally useful. However, entrepreneurs need to separate what they believe about their idea from what they can actually prove.

Consider a student who wants to create an app that helps college students manage their academic schedules. The student assumes that everyone struggles to organise assignments, examinations, and deadlines.

But is that really the problem?

Some students might already use digital calendars. Others might prefer handwritten planners, while some may struggle more with procrastination than organisation.

If the entrepreneur immediately starts building the app, they risk creating something that does not address the most important problem faced by their intended users.

Instead, they should begin by understanding the people they want to help.

They could speak to students, ask how they currently manage their schedules, and identify what frustrates them about existing solutions. These conversations might reveal that students do not need another calendar app. Perhaps they need a simpler way to track assignment deadlines or coordinate group projects.

That discovery could completely change the direction of the idea.

The goal is not to convince people that your idea is good. It is to understand whether your idea solves a problem worth solving.

## 2. Turn Your Assumptions Into Experiments

Once entrepreneurs understand the problem, the next step is to test their assumptions.

Every startup begins with unanswered questions. Will people use the product? Are they willing to pay for it? Does the proposed solution actually make their lives easier?

Instead of treating these assumptions as facts, entrepreneurs can turn them into small experiments.

For example, imagine a student who wants to launch a platform connecting college students with local tutors.

Before building an entire website or application, they could test the idea in simpler ways:

Conduct interviews: Speak to students and parents to understand their tutoring needs, current alternatives, and difficulties. Create a survey: Gather information about preferred subjects, learning formats, and pricing expectations. Build a landing page: Explain the proposed service and invite interested students to register. Run a small pilot: Connect a few students with tutors manually and observe how the process works.

These experiments help entrepreneurs gather evidence without committing substantial resources too early.

However, it is important to ask the right questions. Asking someone, "Would you use my app?" may produce encouraging answers, but those answers do not necessarily predict future behaviour.

People might support an idea because they want to be polite, because it sounds interesting, or because they imagine using it someday.

Questions about their actual experiences are often more useful.

For instance, asking, "How did you find your last tutor?" or "What was the most difficult part of that process?" can reveal genuine needs and existing frustrations.

The purpose of an experiment is not to collect compliments. It is to discover evidence that helps you make better decisions.

## 3. Build an MVP Before Building Everything

Once entrepreneurs have a clearer understanding of the problem, they can begin testing a simple version of their proposed solution.

This brings us to the concept of a Minimum Viable Product (MVP).

An MVP is an early version of a product that includes enough essential functionality to help entrepreneurs test their assumptions and learn from real users.

The idea is simple: instead of building everything at once, start with what is necessary to test whether the solution provides value.

Think about the tutoring platform we discussed earlier.

The founder does not necessarily need a fully developed application with automated payments, advanced search filters, chat features, and personalised recommendations.

Instead, they could begin with a simple website or even a form where students submit their requirements. The founder could then connect those students with suitable tutors manually.

Although this version may not look like a complete business, it can still answer important questions:

Are students interested in the service? Can the platform successfully connect students with tutors? Are students satisfied with their matches? Would they recommend the service to others? Are they willing to pay for the service?

The answers can help the founder decide what to improve before investing in more advanced features.

An MVP is not about creating a low-quality product. It is about building a focused version of the solution that allows meaningful learning.

Build enough to test your assumptions, not so much that changing direction becomes expensive.

This approach is particularly useful for student entrepreneurs and early-stage founders who may have limited budgets, small teams, and competing academic or professional responsibilities.

## 4. Listen to Feedback, but Watch What People Do

Customer feedback is essential during validation, but entrepreneurs must learn to interpret it carefully.

Someone might say that a product is useful without ever using it. Another person might criticise a feature that the founder considers important. Different customers may have completely different expectations.

This is why entrepreneurs should consider both what people say and what they actually do.

Imagine launching an early version of a study-planning tool. Several students sign up because the idea sounds interesting, but only a few return to use it after the first week.

The initial sign-ups suggest curiosity, but the low level of continued use raises another question: Is the product genuinely useful enough to become part of their routine?

Entrepreneurs can investigate by asking users about their experiences, observing how they interact with the product, and identifying where they lose interest.

They can also track useful indicators, such as: User engagement (are people actively using the product?), Retention (do users return after their first experience?), Conversion (do interested users take the next step, such as making a purchase?), Customer satisfaction (does the solution meet users' expectations?), and Referrals (are users recommending the product to others?).

The most relevant indicators depend on the business model and the stage of development. A new product does not need to track every possible metric. It needs to identify the evidence that best answers its most important questions.

Feedback should also lead to action.

If users repeatedly struggle with the same feature, the entrepreneur should investigate whether it needs improvement. If customers consistently request something different from the original concept, the founder may need to reconsider the product's direction.

Listening to customers does not mean implementing every suggestion. It means recognising patterns, understanding the underlying problems, and making informed decisions.

## 5. Learn, Improve, and Test Again

Validation is not a one-time activity that ends as soon as an entrepreneur receives positive feedback.

It is an ongoing process of learning and improvement.

The first experiment may reveal that the original assumption was incorrect. The second might identify a more promising customer group. A third could show that the solution works but needs a different pricing model.

These discoveries are not necessarily failures. They are opportunities to make better decisions before committing more resources.

Consider a startup that initially creates a productivity application for all college students. After speaking to users and testing the product, the founders discover that final-year engineering students are particularly interested in its project-management features.

Instead of trying to serve everyone immediately, they could focus on this specific group, improve the features that matter most to them, and test whether the revised product delivers greater value.

This process of making changes based on evidence is often associated with iteration.

Sometimes, the findings may even lead to a significant change in the business idea. This is known as a pivot — a deliberate change in strategy based on what the founders have learned.

A pivot does not necessarily mean abandoning the original vision. It can mean changing the product, target audience, business model, or approach to solving the problem.

The important thing is to remain open to evidence rather than becoming attached to the original plan.

Entrepreneurs who validate continuously give themselves more opportunities to identify problems early, improve their solutions, and build products that better meet customer needs.

## 6. Common Validation Mistakes to Avoid

Although validation sounds straightforward, several mistakes can make the process less effective.

Confusing compliments with demand: Friends and family may encourage an entrepreneur, but positive comments alone do not establish that a product has a viable market. Look for stronger evidence, such as repeated use, genuine interest, or willingness to pay.

Building too much too soon: Developing a complicated product before testing its core assumptions can waste time and money. Start with the simplest experiment that can answer the most important question.

Ignoring negative feedback: Not every criticism will be useful, but repeatedly hearing the same concern should prompt further investigation. Entrepreneurs must be willing to question their assumptions.

Trying to satisfy everyone: Different customers have different needs. Attempting to please every potential user can make a product unfocused. Start by identifying a specific audience and understanding its most important problems.

Treating validation as a final checkpoint: Customer needs, competitors, and market conditions can change. Validation should continue as the product develops and the business grows.

Avoiding these mistakes helps entrepreneurs use their time more effectively and make decisions based on evidence rather than excitement alone.

![Validation: turn assumptions into evidence, then test, learn and improve](/images/validation-blog-1.jpg)

## From Testing an Idea to Building Something Bigger

Every successful startup begins with an idea, but not every idea becomes a successful business. The difference often lies in the willingness to test assumptions, listen to customers, and improve based on real-world feedback.

Validation helps entrepreneurs move beyond what they think people need and discover what people actually value. It saves time, reduces unnecessary costs, and gives founders a clearer direction before investing heavily in their ideas.

But validation is not about proving that an idea is perfect. It is about learning what works, identifying what does not, and being willing to make changes along the way.

In our journey from Idea to Impact, ideation helped us discover possibilities, and validation helped us test those possibilities against reality. The next step is turning a validated idea into something people can use, trust, and return to.

That brings us to the next stage: Growth — taking an idea from an early version to a product that reaches more people and creates lasting value.

title: From MVP to Market: How Do Entrepreneurs Build and Grow a Startup?
author: Idea Incubator, MGIT
excerpt: Having a great idea is exciting. Testing it and discovering that people actually want it is even better. But what happens after that? This is where growth begins — turning initial interest into something people use regularly.
content:
## Idea to Impact — Stage 3: Growth

Having a great idea is exciting. Testing it and discovering that people actually want it is even better. But what happens after that?

Imagine you're a college student who notices that students around campus struggle to find affordable, homemade food. You come up with an idea for a platform that connects students with local home cooks. You talk to potential users, understand their needs, and discover that many students are genuinely interested.

At this point, you know your idea has potential. But having interested customers and building a successful business are two different things.

How do you turn that initial interest into something people use regularly? How do you find your first customers, improve your product, and grow without running out of money or resources?

This is where growth begins.

![Stage 3, Growth: six steps from building your MVP to creating lasting impact](/images/growth-blog-1.jpeg)

## 1. Start Small, but Start Smart

One of the biggest mistakes first-time entrepreneurs make is trying to build everything at once.

When founders imagine their future business, they often picture a fully developed product with every feature they can think of. However, building everything before understanding what customers actually need can waste both time and money.

Instead, entrepreneurs can begin with a Minimum Viable Product (MVP).

An MVP is the simplest usable version of a product that helps test its core value with real users. It doesn't have to look perfect or include every feature. It simply needs to solve the main problem it was created for.

Let's return to our homemade food platform.

Instead of spending months building an app with online payments, delivery tracking, ratings, and multiple other features, the founder could begin with a simple website or even a WhatsApp-based ordering system.

Students could place orders, home cooks could prepare meals, and the founder could observe what works.

Do students actually order? Which meals are popular? Are customers satisfied with the price and delivery experience?

These early experiences can help the founder understand what deserves improvement before investing heavily in development.

The goal isn't to build the smallest business possible. It's to learn what works before scaling it.

## 2. Find Your First Customers

Building a product is one challenge. Getting people to use it is another.

Even a useful product can struggle if nobody knows it exists. This is why finding the first customers is such an important stage of startup growth.

For new founders, the process doesn't necessarily require expensive advertising campaigns or a large marketing budget.

Sometimes, the best place to start is closer than expected.

A student founder could introduce a product to classmates, college clubs, local communities, or people who experience the problem firsthand. These early users can provide valuable feedback and help the founder understand how the product fits into their daily lives.

However, getting someone to try a product once doesn't automatically mean they will continue using it.

The real questions are: Does the product solve a problem people genuinely care about? Would customers choose it over their existing alternatives? Would they use it again? Would they recommend it to someone else?

These questions help founders look beyond initial excitement and focus on actual customer behaviour.

Early customers aren't just people who buy a product. They can also become an important source of learning.

## 3. Listen, Improve, Repeat

Here's something founders need to understand: your first version probably won't be your best version.

And that's completely normal.

When entrepreneurs begin developing a product, they make assumptions about what customers want. Some assumptions turn out to be correct, while others don't.

The important thing is what they do next.

Imagine that students love the homemade food platform but complain that delivery takes too long. The founder might initially assume that adding more food options will attract more customers. However, customer feedback suggests that improving delivery would make a bigger difference.

If the founder pays attention, they can focus on the problem that matters most.

This process of gathering feedback, making improvements, and testing the results helps a startup become more useful over time.

It also introduces an important concept: product–market fit.

Product–market fit is the point at which a product meets a meaningful market need and customers demonstrate that they genuinely want it. There isn't one universal milestone that proves a startup has achieved it. Founders look for signals such as repeat usage, customer retention, referrals, and consistent demand.

A product doesn't become successful simply because its creators love it. It needs to deliver value to the people it was designed for.

Growth begins with understanding customers, not just convincing them to buy.

## 4. Turn Early Success into Sustainable Growth

Once a startup begins attracting customers and delivering value, the next question is how to grow.

Should the founder reach more people? Introduce new features? Enter another market? Hire a team?

The answer depends on the business.

Growth isn't simply about getting bigger as quickly as possible. It's about expanding in a way the business can actually support.

For example, if our homemade food platform suddenly receives hundreds of orders, the founder needs to consider whether the cooks can handle the demand, whether deliveries will remain reliable, and whether the business can manage its costs.

If the number of customers increases but the quality of service declines, rapid growth may create more problems than opportunities.

Founders need to understand their finances, manage their resources, maintain quality, and build systems that can support increasing demand.

They also need to identify the methods that help them reach the right customers. Depending on the business, this might include referrals, partnerships, social media, content marketing, or paid advertising.

There is no single growth strategy that works for every startup.

What matters is finding an approach that attracts the right customers while allowing the business to deliver consistent value.

Sustainable growth means building a business that can handle success, not just attract attention.

## 5. Growth Doesn't Always Mean Becoming Bigger Overnight

When people hear about startups, they often hear stories of rapid expansion, huge investments, and founders building companies worth millions.

These stories can make growth look like a race.

But every startup has a different journey.

For a student founder, growth might initially mean getting the first ten paying customers. For another entrepreneur, it might mean improving customer retention or earning enough revenue to cover operating expenses.

These milestones may not look impressive from the outside, but they can be important steps towards building a sustainable business.

Entrepreneurs don't always need to chase investment or expand into multiple markets immediately. Sometimes, the smarter decision is to strengthen the product, understand the customers better, and build a reliable foundation.

Investors, media attention, and rapid expansion can create opportunities, but they don't automatically make a startup successful.

What matters is whether the business continues to solve a real problem and create value.

Growth is not just about how far a startup reaches. It's also about how well it serves the people who depend on it.

## 6. Learn to Adapt as You Grow

A startup that works well in its early stages may face completely different challenges as it expands.

A founder who once managed every order personally might eventually need a team. A product designed for a small group of users might need technical improvements to support thousands. A marketing strategy that worked within one college might not work in another city.

As the business changes, the founder must change with it.

This requires more than determination. It requires the ability to recognise mistakes, respond to changing customer needs, manage people, and make decisions based on evidence rather than assumptions.

Sometimes, adapting means improving the original idea. Sometimes, it means changing the business model. And occasionally, it means recognising that a particular approach isn't working and trying something different.

Successful entrepreneurship doesn't mean getting every decision right the first time.

It means learning from decisions and using those lessons to make better ones.

After all, growth is not a straight line. It's a continuous process of testing, learning, improving, and moving forward.

![Growth: how startups build and scale, from first customers to lasting impact](/images/growth-blog-2.jpeg)

## From Idea to Impact

Let's return to where we started: a student with an idea for a homemade food platform.

First, the student notices a problem and develops a possible solution. That's ideation.

Next, the student speaks to potential customers and tests whether the problem and solution are real. That's validation.

Finally, the student builds a simple version of the platform, attracts early customers, learns from their experiences, and improves the business over time. That's growth.

Each stage builds on the previous one.

An idea alone doesn't guarantee a successful business. Validation can show that an opportunity exists, but it doesn't guarantee that a business will survive. Growth requires entrepreneurs to keep delivering value, making informed decisions, and adapting to what they learn.

And this is what makes entrepreneurship more than simply coming up with something new.

It's about taking an idea, understanding the people it could help, and doing the work required to turn that possibility into something meaningful.

Because the real impact of an idea isn't measured by how exciting it sounds at the beginning, but by the value it creates as it grows.
